content: The publication titled Integrating Palliative Care and Symptom Relief into the Response to Humanitarian Emergencies and Crises: A WHO Guide (ISBN 978-92-4-151446-0) was released by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2018. The cover images are credited to various WHO photographers and contributors. The document is part of a series of WHO publications on palliative care, aiming to provide practical guidance on integrating palliative care and symptom relief into health care systems, particularly in the context of humanitarian emergencies and crises. The foreword highlights that humanitarian emergencies and crises often lead to the collapse of health care systems, forced displacement, and widespread suffering, including physical, psychological, social, and spiritual distress. While current responses focus on saving lives, the prevention and relief of pain and other symptoms are equally critical for ethical and medical reasons. Palliative care should be integrated into humanitarian responses to address these needs. The principles of humanitarianism and impartiality demand that all patients receive care, including those who are dying, ensuring that no one is abandoned. The guide outlines the overlap between the principles of palliative care and humanitarianism, including the relief of suffering, respect for human dignity, support for basic needs, and accompaniment during difficult times. It is intended to assist those involved in planning, implementing, or managing responses to humanitarian emergencies, as well as palliative care practitioners interested in contributing to such efforts. WHO reaffirms its commitment to addressing the needs of all people, particularly the most vulnerable. The development of the guide was coordinated by Eric Krakauer under the supervision of Marie-Charlotte Bouësseau and Edward Kelley from the WHO Department of Service Delivery and Safety. The principal writing team included experts from various organizations, such as Médecins Sans Frontières, the International Narcotics Control Board, and Harvard Medical School. WHO acknowledges the valuable contributions of numerous individuals and organizations, as well as the financial support provided by the True Colours Trust. The guide also includes a glossary of abbreviations and acronyms, such as CHC (community health centre), CHS (Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability), EMT (emergency medical team), and others, to facilitate understanding of the content. It provides an expanded conception of palliative care tailored to the needs of those affected by humanitarian emergencies and crises, proposing an Essential Package of Palliative Care for Humanitarian Emergencies and Crises (EP Hum). The introduction notes that nearly 125 million people required humanitarian assistance worldwide in 2015, yet responses to such emergencies rarely include palliative care. This guide, the fourth in a series of WHO documents on palliative care, underscores the medical and moral necessity of integrating palliative care and pain relief into responses to all types of humanitarian emergencies and crises. The concept of humanitarianism is defined as the benevolent response to the suffering and needs of others, aiming to prevent and alleviate human suffering, protect life and health, and ensure respect for human dignity. Motivated by charity, solidarity, or a sense of moral obligation, humanitarianism encompasses responses to suffering caused by disasters, conflicts, health emergencies, or prolonged poverty. It often involves providing health care and social supports, such as food, water, shelter, and education. The historical roots of humanitarianism are traced to the efforts of Henry Dunant, who, moved by the suffering of wounded soldiers after the Battle of Solferino in 1859, initiated the creation of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). The Geneva Conventions, first signed in 1864, form the foundation of international humanitarian law, protecting civilians, health workers, and aid workers, as well as wounded and sick soldiers and prisoners of war. The principles of humanitarianism, as proclaimed by the Red Cross in 1965, include humanity, impartiality, neutrality, and independence. These principles emphasize the prevention and alleviation of suffering, the protection of life and health, and the promotion of mutual understanding and peace. Humanitarianism recognizes the universality of suffering and the moral imperative to respond, respecting human dignity and providing assistance regardless of identity or actions.
